# tree


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

## What a tree adds

A plain chunk store can tell you which 512-byte piece of text matches a
query. It cannot tell you which chapter or section that piece belongs
to, and a piece cut from the middle of a section often makes little
sense on its own. This module records the structure of each document so
search results can be placed and read in context.

At ingest, each document is split into a tree of sections. A node is one
section: the document itself is the root node, and each heading (or
chapter line, or citation, or group of pages) opens a child node below
it. Every node has a `node_id` of the form `<doc id>#<seq>`, where `seq`
is the node’s position in the document. Every chunk is stored with the
`node_id` of the section it came from and its heading path, the chain of
section titles from the document down to that section, such as
`Grahas › Saturn › Sade Sati`. Results call this path the breadcrumb.

With the tree in place you get:

- `doc_search`, hybrid search whose hits carry a breadcrumb and whose
  neighbouring hits in one section are joined;
- `sections`, search that returns the best sections instead of chunks;
- `toc` and `read`, which list a document’s sections and return one
  whole section, without computing any embeddings;
- `context`, which gathers the best sections for a question, with their
  full text, for a language model to read.

Nothing here calls a language model. Node summaries are the first 300
characters of the section unless you pass your own function as
`summarize=`.

[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) (see
the api page) calls all of these for you with its encoder already
chosen. Call them directly when you build your own
[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database).

## Detecting structure

[`build_tree`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#build_tree)
needs to know what marks a new section in a document.
[`detect_mode`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#detect_mode)
looks for four kinds of signal and picks one mode per document:

</tr>
<tr>

<code>#</code> headings</td>

</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>chapter</code></td>
<td>lines like <code>CHAPTER IV</code>, <code>Article 12</code> or
<code>ADHYAYA 3</code></td>
<td>scanned or plain-text books and legislation</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>window</code></td>
<td>every 8 pages</td>
<td>anything with none of the above</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

The window mode is the fallback, so every document gets a tree of some
kind. A document counts as markdown with at least 2 headings if it has
up to 3 pages, and otherwise at least 3 headings or one per 25 pages,
whichever is more, so a one-page note with a single heading becomes one
window. Some PDF converters mark every bold line as a top-level heading.
When a document has more than 4 headings per page, all at the same
depth,
[`detect_mode`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#detect_mode)
does not trust them and uses chapter lines or windows instead.

In chapter mode,
[`struct_levels`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#struct_levels)
decides how the structural words nest. Known words have a fixed order:
BOOK, TITLE, PART and similar come first, then CHAPTER, then SECTION,
then ARTICLE, RULE and CLAUSE. Levels are then renumbered from 1 with no
gaps, so a document that only uses “Article” gets its articles at
level 1. At most 4 levels are kept.

[`detect_mode`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#detect_mode)
checks for verse mode first. It chooses verse when at least 3 pages
carry a citation, citations appear on more than a fifth of the pages,
they name at least two levels (such as chapter and verse), and they
outnumber markdown headings.

### TreeNode

``` python
def TreeNode(
    seq:int, title:str, level:int, parent:int | None=None, page_start:int=0, page_end:int=0, segments:list=<factory>,
    children:list=<factory>, summary:str=''
)->None:
```

*One section of a document, where `seq` is its position in the node list
and `parent` is the `seq` of the section above it.*

[`build_tree`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#build_tree)
takes a list of `(page number, text)` pairs and returns the nodes as a
flat list, where `nodes[seq]` is the node with that `seq` and each
node’s `parent` is its parent’s `seq`. The same list is written to the
`nodes` table, and `toc()` rebuilds the nesting when you ask for it. A
heading is placed under the nearest earlier heading of a shallower
level, so a document that starts at `##` or jumps from `#` to `###`
still nests correctly.

In verse mode, a citation like `Mn_1.1` gives the verse’s address: every
part except the last names the division it belongs to, so `Mn_1.1` opens
a node `Mn 1` for chapter 1. Verse mode also reads `#` headings, because
some texts name their sections (`## dhyanam`) and carry no citations.
Citation levels are counted from the heading above them.

[`heading_path`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#heading_path)
builds the breadcrumb for a node. If a segment repeats the one before
it, it is dropped, so a PDF whose first heading is the same as the
document title reads `Field Manual › Chapter 1` and not
`Field Manual › Field Manual › Chapter 1`.

The breadcrumb is stored with every chunk in the `heading` column, and
by default it is also prepended to the chunk’s text before embedding, so
the vector reflects where the text sits. It is not added to the
full-text index: a keyword search for a section title finds only chunks
whose own text contains it.

### build_tree

``` python
def build_tree(
    pages, # list of (page number, text); the text may be markdown or plain
    title:str='Document', # title of the root node
    summarize:NoneType=None, # function from section text to a summary; None keeps the first 300 characters
    window:int=8, # pages per node in `window` mode
    min_level:int=1, # floor for heading depth
    max_levels:int=4, # deepest node level kept
    mode:str=None, # `markdown`, `verse`, `chapter` or `window`; None detects it
)->list:
```

*Split a document into sections and return them as a flat list of
[`TreeNode`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#treenode),
with the root at index 0.*

``` python
tree = build_tree([(0, '# Saturn\n\nIntro text about the ringed planet.\n\n## Transits\n\nSade sati runs seven years.'),
                   (1, '## Remedies\n\nRecite on Saturdays.')], title='Jyotisha')
for n in tree: print(f'{n.seq}  lvl{n.level}  p{n.page_start}-{n.page_end}  {n.title!r:24} {n.summary[:40]!r}')
assert [n.title for n in tree] == ['Jyotisha', 'Saturn', 'Transits', 'Remedies']
assert tree[2].parent == 1 and tree[3].parent == 1, 'h2s hang off the h1, not off each other'
assert heading_path(tree, tree[2], 'Jyotisha') == 'Jyotisha › Saturn › Transits'
```

    0  lvl0  p0-1  'Jyotisha'               'Saturn'
    1  lvl1  p0-0  'Saturn'                 'Intro text about the ringed planet.'
    2  lvl2  p0-0  'Transits'               'Sade sati runs seven years.'
    3  lvl2  p1-1  'Remedies'               'Recite on Saturdays.'

``` python
# a heading is a heading whatever its first letter: `## verses 6` used to be dropped, shifting the nodes after it
_low = build_tree([(0, '# Book\n\nintro\n\n## verses 1\n\nalpha\n\n## Verses 2\n\nbeta\n\n## verses 6\n\ngamma')], title='Doc')
assert [n.title for n in _low] == ['Doc', 'Book', 'verses 1', 'Verses 2', 'verses 6'], [n.title for n in _low]
assert [n.parent for n in _low] == [None, 0, 1, 1, 1]
assert 'gamma' in _low[4].text() and 'alpha' in _low[2].text()
```

``` python
# a skipped heading level must not nest siblings under each other. Both of these are ordinary
# documents: a README with no h1, so `##` is the shallowest heading, and a document that jumps
# from `#` straight to `###`.
_gap = build_tree([(0, '> a tagline\n\n## Install\n\npip install\n\n'
                      '## Encoders\n\nencoders\n\n### Fallback\n\nhashing')], title='litesearch')
assert [n.title for n in _gap] == ['litesearch', 'Install', 'Encoders', 'Fallback']
assert [n.parent for n in _gap] == [None, 0, 0, 2], [n.parent for n in _gap]
assert heading_path(_gap, _gap[2], 'litesearch') == 'litesearch › Encoders'
assert heading_path(_gap, _gap[3], 'litesearch') == 'litesearch › Encoders › Fallback'

_jump = build_tree([(0, '# Doc\n\ntop\n\n### Deep One\n\na\n\n### Deep Two\n\nb')], title='Doc')
assert [n.parent for n in _jump] == [None, 0, 1, 1], [(n.title, n.level, n.parent) for n in _jump]
```

```` python
# a `#` comment inside a fenced block is a comment, not an h1 — otherwise a README's usage examples
# invent sections that adopt every real heading after them
_readme = '''# vishalakshi

> a tagline

## Harvest

```python
v.apis('https://shop/browse')
# [0] .../api/bff/products?page=1   records: 24
```

## Watches

watch what changes
'''
_fen = build_tree([(0, _readme)], title='vishalakshi')
assert [n.title for n in _fen] == ['vishalakshi', 'vishalakshi', 'Harvest', 'Watches'], [n.title for n in _fen]
assert [n.parent for n in _fen] == [None, 0, 1, 1]
assert 'records: 24' in _fen[2].text(), 'the fenced lines are still text, only never headings'
assert _md_stats([(0, _readme)]) == (3, 2)        # h1 + 2 h2; the comment is not a heading
assert detect_mode([(0, _readme)]) == 'markdown'

# an unclosed fence swallows the rest of the document rather than mis-reading it as structure
_open = build_tree([(0, '# Doc\n\n## Alpha\n\n```\n## Beta\n')], title='Doc')
assert [n.title for n in _open] == ['Doc', 'Doc', 'Alpha'], [n.title for n in _open]
assert '## Beta' in _open[2].text()

# a ````-fenced block quotes ``` blocks inside itself: only a fence at least as long closes it
_nest = '# Doc\n\n## Alpha\n\n````md\n```\n# Not a heading\n```\n````\n\n## Beta\n\nb'
assert [n.title for n in build_tree([(0, _nest)], title='Doc')] == ['Doc', 'Doc', 'Alpha', 'Beta']
# and the two fence characters do not close each other
assert list(_md_lines('~~~\n# x\n```\n# y\n~~~')) == [
    ('~~~', True), ('# x', True), ('```', True), ('# y', True), ('~~~', True)]
````

``` python
# a scanned book has chapter lines, not markdown; and a doc with neither still gets a tree
_book = build_tree([(i, f'CHAPTER {i+1}\n\nbody of chapter {i+1}') for i in range(4)], title='Saravali')
assert detect_mode([(i, f'CHAPTER {i+1}\n\nbody') for i in range(4)]) == 'chapter'
assert len(_book) == 5 and _book[1].title.startswith('CHAPTER 1')

_plain = build_tree([(i, f'page {i} of undifferentiated prose') for i in range(20)], title='Notes', window=8)
assert detect_mode([(i, 'prose') for i in range(20)]) == 'window'
assert len(_plain) == 4, [n.title for n in _plain]   # root + ceil(20/8) windows
assert _plain[1].title.startswith('Pages 1–8')
```

## The tables

`get_tree` adds three tables beside a chunk store and four columns to
the store. The chunk store is still an ordinary store, so full-text
search, the ANN index and `db.search` work on it unchanged.

    docs    id · title · source · kind · pages · meta · hash · added_at
    sources source · doc_id · added_at
    nodes   id ('doc#seq') · doc_id · parent_id · level · seq · title ·
            page_start · page_end · summary · nchunks
    store   content · embedding · metadata · doc_id · node_id · page · heading   [+ FTS5, +ANN]

For the default store the tables are called `docs` and `nodes`; for a
store called `papers` they are `papers_docs`, `papers_sources` and
`papers_nodes`.

A document’s id is a hash of its source and its title. A file’s source
is its resolved path, so a relative path, an absolute path and a symlink
to one file are one source. `hash` is a hash of the document’s
`(page, text)` pairs, and `sources` maps every source to the document
holding its text:

- The same source with the same text again is skipped as `unchanged`.
- The same source with changed text replaces the old chunks and nodes,
  and keeps the id.
- A different source with text already stored is skipped as
  `same text as <source>`, and gains a row in `sources` pointing at the
  stored document. A copy, or a string with the same text, adds no
  chunks.
- A document goes when the last source pointing at it does.
  `delete_source` forgets one source. `delete_doc` forgets the
  document’s own source; text another source shares stays, under that
  source. Editing a file whose text another source shares moves the old
  text to an id of its own for that source first.
- A text added with no `source` is keyed by its title. A second,
  different text under the same title is skipped, as before 0.1.50,
  because a title names nothing on disk.

`force=True` rebuilds a document even when its text is stored, which is
how a new chunker, mode or `meta_fn` reaches text already ingested. A
title or kind change on one source builds a new document under the new
id and drops the old one.

A store written before 0.1.50 has no `sources` table and no hashes.
`get_tree` creates the table and fills it from `docs.source`. Re-adding
a file by the path it was first added under moves its document to the
resolved-path id, keeping its vectors, and re-embeds it once to record
its hash. Duplicates an old store already holds go as their sources are
re-added.

## Ingestion

There are three ways in, from the most control to the least:

- `add_doc` takes text you have already extracted, as a string or a list
  of `(page number, text)` pairs. It builds the tree, chunks each
  section, embeds the chunks with `emb_fn` and stores them. Use it when
  your app fetches or converts documents itself.
- `add_file` reads one file and passes its pages to `add_doc`.
- `add_dir` does the same for every document file under a folder, or for
  a list of files.

Each returns a dict per document with its
[`doc_id`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#doc_id),
`title`, `kind`, number of `nodes` and number of `chunks`, or a
`skipped` reason when its text is already stored: `unchanged`, or
`same text as <source>`.

`emb_fn` takes a list of strings and returns one vector per string.
Without it, chunks are stored with no embedding, which is enough for
keyword search, `toc` and `read`.

Chunks are cut within each section, never across a section boundary,
using
[`chunk_markdown`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#chunk_markdown)’s
default chunker unless you pass `chunker=`, any chonkie chunker. A chunk
shorter than 40 characters is joined to the chunk before it instead of
being stored alone. Two chunks with the same text in different sections
are both kept, because the row id is a hash of the node id and the text.

A chunker sees one segment of a section at a time. Some readers produce
very small segments, such as one verse per page, and a chunker aiming at
700 characters never reaches that size on a 60-character verse. A
chunker can ask for its small chunks to be joined across segments by
having `pack_cited=True` and a `target` size;
[`pack_target`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#pack_target)
reads the size a chunker asks for, and
[`_pack_segments`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#_pack_segments)
then joins consecutive chunks of one node up to `target` characters.
Ordinary chunkers have neither attribute and are unaffected.

`add_doc(defer=...)` collects the chunks in a list instead of embedding
and storing them, and
[`store_chunks`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#store_chunks)
embeds and stores such a list later. `add_doc(jobs=...)` collects the
whole write, and `_commit` stores a batch of them: chunks first, then
nodes, doc rows and sources. `add_dir` uses this to embed chunks from
many documents in batches of 2,000 (`embed_batch`), which is faster than
one call per document, and a run that fails before a batch is stored
leaves the documents it would have replaced whole.

### Database.add_doc

``` python
def add_doc(
    pages, # list of (page number, text), or one string
    title:str, # document title
    source:str=None, # path or url; an existing path is stored resolved. None keys the text by its title
    kind:str='text', # a label stored on the doc row to filter on, such as 'pdf', 'web' or 'md'
    store:str='store', # chunk store
    prefix:str=None, # tree table prefix
    emb_fn:NoneType=None, # function from a list of strings to vectors; None stores no embeddings
    chunker:NoneType=None, # chonkie chunker; None uses chunk_markdown's default
    summarize:NoneType=None, # function from section text to a summary
    with_heading:bool=True, # embed each chunk together with its heading path
    meta:dict=None, # arbitrary json metadata for the doc row
    force:bool=False, # rebuild the document even when its text is already stored
    index:bool=True, # mirror this document's chunks into the ANN index
    mode:str=None, # force a build_tree structural mode instead of detecting one
    meta_fn:NoneType=None, # (chunk text) -> dict of facets stored as the chunk's `metadata`
    defer:list=None, # collect chunks here instead of embedding and storing them
    jobs:list=None, # collect the whole write here for `_commit`, as `add_dir` does
)->dict:
```

*Ingest one document: build its tree, chunk each section, embed the
chunks and store them.*

### pack_target

``` python
def pack_target(
    chunker
)->int:
```

*Return the size a chunker asks consecutive segments to be joined up to,
or 0 to chunk each segment on its own.*

`add_file` handles document files: PDF, markdown, plain text,
reStructuredText, notebooks, XML, HTML and CoNLL-U. XML, HTML and
CoNLL-U are read as plain text unless a registered profile claims them.
A PDF is converted to one markdown page per PDF page by
[`pdf_parse`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pdf_parse),
and its images are saved under `db.assets()`, a folder beside the
database file. A notebook becomes one page with its cells joined. Any
other file is read as one page of text. The title defaults to the file
name with underscores and hyphens turned into spaces, and `kind`
defaults to the extension (`notebook` for `.ipynb`).

Source code does not fit a heading-based tree. To index code, use
[`Index.add_code`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index.add_code)
(see the api page), which cuts it into top-level functions and classes
using Python’s syntax tree.

A [`Profile`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#profile)
(see the data page) describes how to read one kind of document: its
parser, chunker, tree mode and per-chunk metadata. When a registered
profile claims a file, `add_file` uses it instead of the steps above.
This is how a TEI edition of a Sanskrit text is told apart from any
other `.xml` file. Pass `profile=` with a name to choose a profile
directly, which is the only way to reach one that cannot be detected
from the file.

``` python
from fastcore.test import test_eq
test_eq(_n_parse_workers([Path(f'p{i}.html') for i in range(8)], None), 0)
test_eq(_n_parse_workers([Path(f'p{i}.pdf') for i in range(4)], None), defaults.cpus)
test_eq(_n_parse_workers([Path('a.html')], 3), 3)
```

`add_dir` ingests every file under `dir` whose extension is in `types`,
or exactly the paths in `files=`. Files whose text is already stored are
skipped, and a file edited since it was added is replaced. Each call
writes to one store, because the embedder and the ANN index belong to
that store; to send files from one folder to different stores, call it
once per store with `files=`.

Parsing PDFs, notebooks and XML is slow, so when 4 or more such files
are in the batch, `add_dir` parses them in a pool of worker processes
(`n_workers` overrides this; 0 means no pool). In one measurement,
parsing took 3.55 of the 5.31 seconds needed to ingest 8 PDFs, while 150
markdown files took 2.7 milliseconds to read in total, too little for a
pool to help, and HTML is read the same way. All writes stay in the main
process.

By default the full-text index is updated as each chunk is written. With
`bulk=True`, `add_dir` turns that off during the load and rebuilds the
full-text index once at the end. This is faster for a large first load,
but keyword search misses the new documents until the load finishes, so
use it only when nothing searches the store meanwhile. The ANN index is
rebuilt once at the end either way.

`stop` is a callable `add_dir` asks before each file, for a caller that
may need to cancel a long load. When it returns True, `add_dir` stops:
the files already stored stay stored and indexed, a parse in flight
finishes, and no further parse starts. Given `stop`, the result is an
`L` whose `cancelled` says whether files went unread and whose `unread`
lists them. Without `stop`, the result is the plain list it always was.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/Karthik777/litesearch/blob/main/litesearch/tree.py#L596"
target="_blank" style="float:right; font-size:smaller">source</a>

### Database.add_dir

``` python
def add_dir(
    dir:NoneType=None, # directory to walk; ignored when `files` is given
    types:str='.pdf,.md,.markdown,.txt,.rst,.ipynb,.xml,.tei,.htm,.html,.conllu', # comma-separated extensions to ingest
    store:str='store', prefix:str=None,
    n_workers:int=None, # parse workers; 0 is serial, None picks by parse-heavy file count
    embed_batch:int=2000, # chunks embedded and written per flush; 0 writes per document
    files:NoneType=None, # ingest exactly these paths instead of walking `dir`
    bulk:bool=False, # rebuild the full-text index once at the end instead of per chunk
    stop:NoneType=None, # asked before each file; True stops, and the result's `unread` holds the rest
    **kw
)->list: # forwarded to add_doc
```

*Ingest every document file under a folder, or a given list of files,
skipping those already ingested; given `stop`, the result is an `L`
carrying `cancelled` and `unread`.*

``` python
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from litesearch.core import database
with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    Path(d, 'a.md').write_text('# Alpha\n\npolonium report')
    x = database(Path(d)/'test.db', sem_search=False)
    x.add_dir(d, types='md')
    assert x.t.store.fts_search('polonium')
```

``` python
with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    Path(d, 'a.md').write_text('# Alpha\n\npolonium report')
    Path(d, 'b.md').write_text('# Beta\n\nthorium report')

    x = database(Path(d)/'test.db', sem_search=False)
    x.add_dir(d, types='md', bulk=True)

    assert len(x.t.store.fts_search('polonium')) == 1
    assert len(x.t.store.fts_search('thorium')) == 1

    # Triggers were restored after the rebuild.
    x.t.store.insert({'content': 'later radium report'})
    assert len(x.t.store.fts_search('radium')) == 1
```

``` python
from fastcore.test import test_eq
with TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    for n in 'abcd': Path(d, f'{n}.md').write_text(f'# {n}\n\n{n} report')
    x, asked = database(Path(d)/'test.db', sem_search=False), []
    def stop(): asked.append(1); return len(asked) > 2
    r = x.add_dir(d, types='md', stop=stop)
    test_eq([o['title'] for o in r], ['a', 'b'])
    assert r.cancelled and [p.name for p in r.unread] == ['c.md', 'd.md']
    assert len(x.t.store.fts_search('report')) == 2, 'what was stored before the stop stays searchable'
    r = x.add_dir(d, types='md', stop=lambda: False)
    assert not r.cancelled and not r.unread
    test_eq(sorted(o['title'] for o in r), ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'])
    assert type(x.add_dir(d, types='md')) is list, 'no stop, no change'
    y, asked = database(Path(d)/'pool.db', sem_search=False), []
    r = y.add_dir(d, types='md', n_workers=2, stop=stop)
    assert r.cancelled and len(r) == 2 and len(r.unread) == 2, 'the pool path stops between files too'
    r = y.add_dir(files=[], stop=lambda: True)
    assert not r.cancelled and not r.unread and not r
```

## Reading the structure

These functions read the tree and compute no embeddings, so they are
fast and need no encoder. They suit an agent or a reader that browses:
look at the table of contents, pick “the chapter on remedies”, and open
it.

- `toc(doc)` returns each document’s tree as nested dicts with node ids,
  titles, levels, page ranges, chunk counts and summaries. `doc` may be
  a doc id or part of a title; leave it out for every document.
  `max_depth` (3) limits how deep it goes.
- `read(node_id)` returns one whole section: its chunks joined in order,
  with the text of all its subsections by default (`children=False` for
  just the section), up to `max_chars` (20,000). It also returns the
  breadcrumb, page range, summary and the ids of its direct children.
- `breadcrumb(node_id)` returns just the title path.

## Retrieval that knows about structure

Hybrid search runs two searches and combines them. The keyword search
uses SQLite FTS5, a full-text index ranked by bm25, which favours chunks
that contain the query’s rarer words. The vector search compares the
query’s embedding with each chunk’s embedding. Reciprocal Rank Fusion
(RRF) merges the two ranked lists: each chunk scores `1/(rrf_k + rank)`
in each list it appears in, so a chunk ranked well by both searches
beats one ranked well by only one. `rrf_k` defaults to 60.

`doc_search` is `db.search` for a tree store, with two additions. Every
hit gets a `breadcrumb`. And hits from the same section at most `gap`
pages apart (1 by default) are joined into one hit, so a reader gets one
passage instead of two halves; the joined hit keeps the best rank and
score of its parts and counts them in `_nspan`. `rerank=True` reorders
the top 30 candidates with a flashrank cross-encoder, a small model that
reads the query and each chunk together; it is slower and downloads a 3
MB model on first use.

`sections` answers “which sections match”, returning sections instead of
chunks. It gathers chunk hits (`limit × fanout`, at least 20), groups
them by node, and scores each section by its best hit (`score='max'`).
Each section comes with its breadcrumb, summary, page range, up to `per`
snippets and a `read` string naming the call that opens it.
`score='mean'` averages the hits and `score='sum'` adds them. Summing
favours long sections that collect many weak hits: on 150 known-item
queries over 486 pages of EU legislation (`07_doc_eval`), sections
scored 0.852 MRR with `sum` against 0.957 with `max` on verbatim
queries, and 0.304 against 0.505 on reworded ones.

Use `doc_search` when you want passages to show or quote. Use `sections`
when the answer is a place in a document, such as which article or
chapter, and you will `read` it next.

`doc_search(adaptive=True)` changes the weight of each list before
fusion using
[`adaptive_weights`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#adaptive_weights),
three fixed rules: when one search returns nothing, the other gets all
the weight; a quoted phrase adds 0.6 to the keyword weight; and a query
where at least half the words look like names or identifiers
(capitalised, containing digits or underscores) adds 0.4. It is off by
default because on the natural-language queries in `07_doc_eval` the
rules never fired.

```

*Return `(fts_weight, vec_weight)` for fusion, from the shape of the

`context` gathers what a language model needs to answer a question from
a document collection, in one call. It returns
`AttrDict(query, results, related)`:

- `results` holds up to `sections` (6) of the best sections. Each has
  its full text from `read` (up to `max_read`, 6,000 characters),
  breadcrumb, pages, summary, score, snippets, source file name, and
  with `tree_ctx=True` its place in the tree from `node_context`: its
  parent, up to 8 sibling sections and up to 12 child sections. A
  document’s root node is never returned as a result, and two sections
  with the same breadcrumb are returned once.
- `related` holds up to `related` (8) other sections that came up in a
  second hybrid search, with their title and breadcrumb but no text. Set
  `vector=False` to skip it.

Extra keyword arguments such as `ann`, `rerank`, `fts_pre` and `rrf_k`
are passed to every search it runs.

## End to end

The example below ingests a short document with two chapters, using
[`hash_embed`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/utils.html#hash_embed)
as the encoder so the notebook runs without downloading a model, and
calls each function in turn.

``` python
import numpy as np, hashlib
from litesearch.core import database
from litesearch.utils import hash_embed

DOC = """# Saturn

Saturn is the slowest of the classical grahas.

## Sade Sati

Sade sati is the seven and a half year period when Saturn transits the twelfth, first and second
houses from the natal moon. It is counted in three phases of roughly thirty months each.

The middle phase, with Saturn over the moon itself, is held to be the heaviest.

## Remedies

Recitation on Saturdays is the common prescription. Donation of black sesame is another.

# Jupiter

Jupiter is the great benefic and moves through one sign each year.

## Transits

Jupiter's return to its natal sign happens roughly every twelve years."""

db  = database()
enc = lambda ts, **kw: hash_embed(ts, 256)
db.get_tree('store')
print(db.add_doc(DOC, title='Grahas', source='notes/grahas.md', kind='md', emb_fn=enc))
```

    {'doc_id': '5a991f283775ae0d', 'title': 'Grahas', 'kind': 'md', 'nodes': 6, 'chunks': 5}

``` python
# the tree came out of the headings, and every chunk knows which node it lives in
t = db.toc('Grahas')[0]
def show(n, d=0):
    print('  '*d + f"{n['title']:<14} chunks={n['nchunks']}  {n['id']}")
    for c in n.get('children', []): show(c, d+1)
show(t['tree'])
assert [c['title'] for c in t['tree']['children']] == ['Saturn', 'Jupiter']
assert db.breadcrumb(t['tree']['children'][0]['children'][0]['id']) == 'Grahas › Saturn › Sade Sati'
```

    Grahas         chunks=0  5a991f283775ae0d#0
      Saturn         chunks=1  5a991f283775ae0d#1
        Sade Sati      chunks=1  5a991f283775ae0d#2
        Remedies       chunks=1  5a991f283775ae0d#3
      Jupiter        chunks=1  5a991f283775ae0d#4
        Transits       chunks=1  5a991f283775ae0d#5

``` python
# read() returns the section, not a fragment -- and includes its children
sec = first(t['tree']['children'][0]['children'], lambda c: c['title'] == 'Sade Sati')
r = db.read(sec['id'])
print(r['breadcrumb'], '|', r['pages'], '|', len(r['text']), 'chars')
assert 'thirty months' in r['text'] and r['breadcrumb'].endswith('Sade Sati')
```

    Grahas › Saturn › Sade Sati | (0, 0) | 266 chars

``` python
# hybrid search, but every hit is placed in the document
q  = 'how long does the saturn transit last'
hits = db.doc_search(q, enc([q])[0].tobytes(), limit=3, dtype=np.float16)
for h in hits: print(f"{h['_rrf_score']:.4f}  {h['breadcrumb']:<28} {h['content'][:60]!r}")
assert hits and all(h['breadcrumb'] for h in hits)

# sections() rolls the same evidence up a level and hands back the next call
secs = db.sections(q, enc([q])[0].tobytes(), limit=2, dtype=np.float16)
for s in secs: print(f"{s['score']:.4f}  {s['breadcrumb']:<28} {s['read']}")
assert secs and secs[0]['read'].startswith('read(')
```

_rq  = 'how long does the saturn transit last'
_rqv = enc([_rq])[0].tobytes()
_plain = db.doc_search(_rq, _rqv, limit=3, dtype=np.float16)
_rr    = db.doc_search(_rq, _rqv, limit=3, dtype=np.float16, rerank=True)
assert len(_rr) <= 3 and all(h['breadcrumb'] for h in _rr)
assert [h['_rrf_score'] for h in _rr] == [1.0/(60+i) for i in range(len(_rr))]
assert [h['_rrf_score'] for h in _plain] != [1.0/(60+i) for i in range(len(_plain))]
# and the roll-up inherits it: sections forwards rerank to the chunk hits it groups
_srr = db.sections(_rq, _rqv, limit=2, dtype=np.float16, rerank=True)
assert _srr and all(s['breadcrumb'] for s in _srr)
print('reranked:', [h['content'][:40] for h in _rr])

# adaptive fusion: a quoted phrase leans on FTS, an empty FTS leg hands the vote to vectors
assert adaptive_weights('"sade sati"', [1], [1])[0] > adaptive_weights('how long does it last', [1], [1])[0]
assert adaptive_weights('anything', [], [1]) == (0.0, 1.0)
assert adaptive_weights('anything', [1], []) == (1.0, 0.0)

# spans: two hits one page apart in the same node become one passage
_h = [dict(content='first half', node_id='d#1', page=3, _rrf_score=0.02, rowid=1),
      dict(content='second half', node_id='d#1', page=4, _rrf_score=0.01, rowid=2),
      dict(content='elsewhere',   node_id='d#9', page=40, _rrf_score=0.005, rowid=3)]
_m = merge_spans(_h)
assert len(_m) == 2 and _m[0]['_nspan'] == 2 and 'second half' in _m[0]['content'], _m
assert _m[0]['_rrf_score'] == 0.02, 'a merged span keeps its best score, it does not accumulate'

# ingestion is content-addressed, and delete_doc leaves nothing behind
again = db.add_doc(DOC, title='Grahas', source='notes/grahas.md', emb_fn=enc)
assert 'skipped' in again, again
did = t['doc_id']
n_before = len(db.t.store())
db.delete_doc(did)

## Limits

- No language model is used. A summary per node is what `toc()` shows a
  reader deciding where to look, and the default is only the first 300
  characters. Pass `summarize=` to write better ones.
- Chunk size matters more than anything else in this module. In
  `07_doc_eval`, cutting smaller chunks instead of page-sized ones
  raised MRR on reworded queries from 0.354 to 0.532, while breadcrumbs
  in the embedding and span joining changed it by less than 0.01. The
  default chunker is
  [`chunk_markdown`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#chunk_markdown);
  pass a better splitter as `chunker=`.

``` python
import tempfile
_d = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(_d/'ratios.md').write_text('# Ratios\n\n## Liquidity\n\nCurrent ratio is current assets over current liabilities.')
(_d/'notes.txt').write_text('A plain text file with no headings at all, ingested as one windowed node.')
_fdb = database()
_fdb.get_tree('store')
print(_fdb.add_dir(_d, emb_fn=enc))
assert {d['title'] for d in _fdb.toc()} == {'ratios', 'notes'}
